formulas.name: Risk priority number (RPN)
formulas.expression: RPN = severity rating x probability rating x detection rating

symbols.severity rating: normalized score for severity of impact of a failure
symbols.probability rating: probability score for likelihood the failure will occur
symbols.detection rating: probability score for likelihood current controls detect the cause/effect

formulas.conditions: Used within FMEA (Failure Mode Effects Analysis) to rank failure modes; plotted in a Pareto chart to prioritize attention.

formulas.name: Average yield per defect opportunity (benchmarking)

symbols.#opportunities: number of opportunities for defects per unit

formulas.conditions: Used to compare dissimilar products made using the same process on a level field regardless of complexity (quantitative benchmarking).

symbols.# defects observed: count of defects found at a process step
symbols.# units: count of units passed through that step

formulas.name: Throughput yield (TY)
formulas.expression: Throughput yield = 1 - Defects/unit (fraction of units passing with zero defects at that step)

symbols.Defects/unit: defects observed divided by units at the step

formulas.conditions: TY is defect-sensitive and measures how well a process is performing at a given point; example: defects/unit = 5% -> throughput yield = 95%.

formulas.name: Defects per opportunity and DPMO

symbols.opportunities/unit: number of CTQ opportunities for defect per unit

formulas.conditions: Example: Defects/unit=0.05, opportunities/unit=20 -> Defects/opportunity=0.0025 -> DPMO=2,500 (about 4.3 sigma capability).

formulas.name: Rolled throughput yield (RTY)
formulas.expression: RTY = TY1 x TY2 x TY3 x ... x TYn

symbols.n: number of steps in the process

formulas.conditions: = probability of passing a unit through all steps defect-free. Example (5-step process): TYs = 98%, 93%, 95%, 98%, 94% -> RTY = (.98)x(.93)x(.95)x(.98)x(.94) = 0.7976.

formulas.name: Normalized yield (NY)
formulas.expression: NY = kth root of RTY, where k is the # steps in the process

symbols.k: number of steps in the process

formulas.conditions: Average throughput yield at any given step. Example as printed: 10-step process, RTY = 36.8% (0.368); NY = (0.368)**(-10) = 0.9051 (see ambiguities: exponent notation as printed does not algebraically reproduce 0.9051 unless the intended exponent is 1/10, i.e. the 10th root).

formulas.name: Units to produce one defect-free output, given RTY
formulas.expression: Repairable defects: 1 + (1 - RTY); Scrapped defectives: 1 / RTY

constant_tables.name: Table 11-1: Process Optimization Tools
rows: Suppliers-Inputs-Process-Outputs-Customers. Create a high-level process map with a few key details about each of the key contributing elements.
Critical to . . . tree. Identify, organize, and display parts of the process according to areas of critical importance.
Define and design processes, including the flow of work or material, the timing of activities, resources consumed, and points of decision, inspection, and delivery.

Simulate the flow of work and material through a process based on the model, and analyze the results of the simulation for overall effectiveness and efficiency. Find defects, errors, bottlenecks, variation, and non value-added elements.
For the outcomes of any process, define all the contributors, weight their effects, and determine the significant contributors to the outputs.
Create a high-level C&E in the form of a tree structure, with categories for each major type of contributor. A method for capturing potential causes and inputs to a process.
For any activity or item, define the potential failure modes, including the likelihood of occurrence, and the ability to detect and characterize the effects of those failures.
Analyze the tradeoffs between product complexity and process capability, and define the proper configuration of each to achieve desired outcomes.
Use the outputs of simulation and analysis to define how data will be collected and how the processes will be controlled and audited.

constant_tables.name: Table 11-2: The SIPOC
rows: Suppliers are systems, people, organizations, or other sources of the materials, information, or other resources that are consumed or transformed in the process.
Inputs are materials, information, and other resources provided by the suppliers that are consumed or transformed in the process.
The process is the set of actions and activities that transform the inputs into the outputs.
Outputs are the products or services produced by the process and used by the customer.
Customers are persons, groups of people, companies, systems, and downstream processes that receive the output of the process.

rows: The basic and descriptive statistics, such as averages, ranges, variance, and so on, used routinely in Six Sigma analysis
Specific tools for analyzing results of data collected over time -- trends, decompositions, moving averages
Analyze variances, test for equality of variances, and determine whether there is a valid relationship between variables.
The analysis of margins and tolerances to determine optimal design specifications
Systematically investigate the process or product variables that affect product quality
Determination of the capability of a process to perform to expectations. The output is a numerically defined index of capability.
Determining the strength of the relationship between a response variable (Y) and one or more predictors (Xs).
The analysis of data from multiple measurements on various items or subjects. The output is a graphical picture of the various relationships.
Methods used to explore data before applying more traditional statistical analysis tools
The analysis of the measurement system to determine the accuracy and precision of the data obtained from the measurement.
Accelerated life testing, lifetime characteristics analysis, growth curves

constant_tables.name: Table 11-7: Plots and Charts
rows: A bar chart that plots the spread of data into bins according to frequency of occurrence, immediately suggesting the distribution function.
A type of histogram where data are displayed in a single-point format; used to assess a distribution or compare distributions.
A bar chart in which the bars are ordered from highest to lowest, showing the critical contributors.
Shows the relationship between two variables, immediately conveying the nature of correlation.
A matrix of scatter-plots, showing the relationships between many pairs of variables at the same time.
A three-dimensional scatter plot, useful for evaluating the relationships between three different variables at the same time.
A two-dimensional plot of data values with added confidence intervals or error bars; useful for showing both the central tendency and the variability.
A side-by-side comparison of sample distributions. By convention, the central line is the mean, the boxes are +/-25%, and the lines are the limits.
A stepped cumulative histogram (without bars), overlaid with a best-fit normal cumulative distribution function. Used to fit a distribution to your data.
A scatter plot, overlaid with a CDF cumulative probability line. Used to determine how closely a particular distribution fits your data.
A plot of data spread over time. Used to evaluate patterns in activity across time. By convention, time is plotted on the x-axis.
A scatter plot with an added histogram (or sometimes a box plot), used to assess the relationship between two variables and their distributions.

constant_tables.name: Table 11-8: Process Capability Analysis Tools
rows: Analyze process capability when the data are from a normal distribution.
Analyze process capability when the data are from a non-normal distribution.
Analyze process capability for between-subgroup and within-subgroup variation.
Analyze the capability of an in-control process when each of multiple continuous variables follow a normal distribution.
Analyze the process when the data are from a binomial distribution -- when examining the number of defective items out of the total number of items sampled.
Analyze the number of defects observed, where the item occupies a specified time or space.
An set of six charts, which collectively contain key process capability metrics.

constant_tables.name: Table 12-1: The Tools of Leadership Communications
rows: The most powerful leadership tool is your personal communication. Direct interaction is the best way to listen and influence.
Using a presentation tool like PowerPoint, a formal presentation is a common, effective, and repeatable leadership and communication tool.
White boards and flip charts make ideal platforms for conveying important ideas and information, conducting brainstorming sessions, developing early designs, and troubleshooting.

Messages, directives, requests, and reports can all be communicated via e-mail, which communicates directly and by passing along different audiences. Using attached files, e-mail is a powerful communication conduit. It's poor and inappropriate for resolving issues, however.
Systems like intranets, file servers, groupware, and enterprise application systems help communicate broadly and consistently.
Particularly when there's an issue or problem, there's nothing quite as effective as just picking up the phone and calling them.
Formal memoranda and letters are most useful for communicating in an official manner, such as a policy directive or formal announcement.
Hey, whatever it takes! Just make sure you get the message out.

constant_tables.name: Table 12-2: Six Sigma Project Management Tools
rows: Capture ideas for potential Six Sigma projects.
Establish the project scope, write a problem and objective statement, set a schedule, and assign initial team members.
Establish priorities for projects, manage the queue of projects, and launch projects.
Track and manage project progress. Identify and manage variance to plan. Ensure deliverables to the established objectives and schedule.
Communicate the status and results of the project -- to the project team members, business owners, Six Sigma Champions, executives, and other constituents.

constant_tables.name: Table 12-3: Basic Elements of Project Definition
rows: The reason and motivation for doing the project. This includes a precise statement of the problem, and its impacts.
The core set of objectives that must be met if the project is to be judged a success. Be quantitative in identifying the anticipated levels of improvement.
How everyone will gain from successfully meeting the project objectives. For Six Sigma projects, this specifically includes the bottom-line benefits.

Identify the team of individuals and skills needed to complete project. The team should be small to remain agile, yet have the sufficient expertise and representation. Typically, a core team of six or fewer are required, with additional help on a part-time basis.
The schedule includes the total duration of the project as well as the individual duration of each project phase

Scope, schedule, and objectives hang in a delicate balance. A change in any one affects at least one of the other two. Estimate the risk and impact of possible and probable changes, and identify the controls you apply to prevent them from occurring and to respond if they do.

given.description: Figure 11-7: Pareto chart of an FMEA risk priority number (RPN), showing counts and cumulative percentage for process outputs such as 'Order Completed on time', 'Billing Accuracy', 'No Production Defects', 'Minimization Cost', 'No Wrong Order Defects'.

conventions.as_stated: All processes vary around their target mean. Over time, the variance increases due to 'process-centering error'. Research has shown that 4-sigma processes drift about 1.5-sigma over time. So when a company claims 6-sigma processes, they really mean: (a) the short-term sigma capability of their processes is 6-sigma (b) the long-term performance is 4.5-sigma due to process-centering errors.

conventions.topic: Sigma level <-> DPMO / cost of quality table
conventions.as_stated: The Cost of Quality: Sigma Level 2 = 308,537 dpm (noncompetitive companies), cost not applicable; 3 = 66,807 dpm, 25-40% of sales; 4 = 6,210 dpm (industry average), 15-25% of sales; 5 = 233 dpm, 5-15% of sales; 6 = 3.4 dpm (world class), <1% of sales. Each sigma shift provides a 10 percent net income improvement, a 20 percent margin improvement, and a 10 to 30 percent capital reduction.

conventions.as_stated: Glossary: 'DPMO (defects per million opportunities): The total number of defects observed divided by the total number of opportunities, expressed in events per million. Sometimes called Defects per Million (DPM)'; 'DPU (defects per unit): The total number of defects detected in some number of units divided by the total number of those units.'; 'opportunities: The number of characteristics, parameters, or features of a product or service that can be classified as acceptable or unacceptable.'; 'defect: An output of a process that fails to meet a defined specification or requirement...'; 'defective: A unit of product or service that contains at least one defect.' Also: Defects Per Million Opportunities defined as the total number of defects per unit divided by the total number of opportunities for defects per unit, multiplied by 1,000,000 (project-selection metric).

Glossary: 'Cp: A capability measure defined as the ratio of the specification width to short-term process performance width.' 'Cpk: An adjusted short-term capability index that reduces the capability score in proportion to the offset of the process center from the specification target.'

Glossary: 'long-term variation: The observed variation of an input or output characteristic that has had the opportunity to experience the majority of the variation effects that influence it.' 'short-term variation: The amount of variation observed in a characteristic that has not had the opportunity to experience all the sources of variation from the inputs acting on it.'

Glossary: 'Black Belt: An individual who receives approximately four weeks of training in the Six Sigma DMAIC methodology, analytical problem solving, and change management methods. A Black Belt is a full time Six Sigma team leader solving problems under the direction of a Six Sigma Champion.' 'Green Belt: ...approximately two weeks of training... a part time Six Sigma practitioner...' 'Master Black Belt (MBB): An individual who has received additional training beyond Black Belt. The MBB is a technical, go-to expert for technical and project issues in Six Sigma...' 'Yellow Belt: An individual who receives approximately one week of training in Six Sigma problem solving and process optimization methods...' 'Champion: A Six Sigma leader, who recognizes, defines, assigns, and supports the successful completion of Six Sigma projects...' Comparison table (Harry & Schroeder outline): Champions=1 week training, 1 per business group/site; Master Black Belts=two 1-week sessions, 1 per 30 Black Belts; Black Belts=four 1-week sessions with assigned project, 1 per 100 employees; 'Green Berets' [as printed, likely Green Belts]=two 3-day sessions with assigned project, 1 per 20 employees.

conventions.topic: DMAIC vs other roadmaps (Harry's Breakthrough Strategy phases)
conventions.as_stated: Glossary: 'DMAIC: The acronym for the five core phases of the Six Sigma methodology: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control; used to solve process and business problems through data and analytical methods.' Harry & Schroeder outline: 'Four core phases in applying Breakthrough Strategy to achieve 6Sigma results: (1) Measure: data collection and reporting (2) Analyze: statistical methods and tools to "explain" defects (3) Improve: "Design for Six Sigma" process (4) Control: continuous monitoring, no problem reoccurrences.' Book summary: 'There are eight phases involved in applying the Breakthrough Strategy...: Recognize, Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control, Standardize and Integrate', grouped into four categories: Identification (Recognize, Define), Characterization (Measure, Analyze), Optimization (Improve, Control), Institutionalization (Standardize, Integrate).

ambiguities.issue: Normalized Yield (NY) example: printed formula 'NY = kth root of TRY... = (0.368)**(-10) = 0.9051' -- the exponent as printed (-10) does not algebraically reproduce 0.9051; 0.368 raised to the 1/10 power (the 10th root) equals approximately 0.9051, suggesting the intended notation was a 1/10 (10th-root) exponent rather than -10. Transcribed exactly as printed per instructions.

Figure 11-7 (Pareto chart of FMEA risk priority number) shows numeric count and percentage labels on bars/curve that are too small/low-resolution to transcribe reliably; not transcribed as data to avoid inventing numbers.
Figure 11-5 (C&E matrix example) shows a filled-in worksheet with numeric ratings, totals and percentages that are too small/low-resolution to transcribe reliably; not transcribed as data.

Figure 12-4 (Balanced Scorecard example) contains a metric row labeled 'TROCE' (appears in the book's own index as 'TROCE, 234'); likely intended as 'ROCE' (return on capital employed) with a stray leading T, or a genuine acronym used by the source. Recorded as printed; numeric values in the figure are too small to transcribe reliably.

'Comparison of Roles' table row for the fourth belt level is labeled 'GREEN BERETS' in the source notes (Six-Sigma Mikel Harry - Richard Schroeder.pdf, page 9); this is almost certainly meant to be 'Green Belts' (matching usage everywhere else in the same document), but is transcribed exactly as printed.

Glossary term for the fishbone/cause-and-effect diagram is printed as 'lshikawa diagram' (lowercase L in place of capital I) due to the book's decorative/garbled font rendering; recorded under the topic name 'Ishikawa diagram' for indexing but the literal glyph in the source page differs.
